about: The single source of the accountable-passive detector's word lists. scripts/gen-agency-lexicon.mjs writes it into the JavaScript, Python and Go engines between BEGIN and END GENERATED AGENCY LEXICON markers, and its --check (run by test/agency-lexicon.test.mjs) fails when any engine's copy drifts. A mark needs all of: a past passive auxiliary; at most one adverb; a participle from one of the classes; the head word its class names, when it names one; no 'by' in the next byWindow words of the clause; the participle's requires and unless conditions; and no negator anywhere in its clause before the auxiliary, that is after the last headStops character before it, or from the start of the text (an n't contraction counts as a negator wherever a negator does). The matcher reads an ASCII-lowercased copy of the text, so every word here is lowercase ASCII, and a phrasal participle is written with one space. The three character sets are written here too, so --check covers them: whitespace separates the words of a match and of a requires or unless phrase; the head walk never crosses a headStops character, and a headStops character starts the clause the negator reader reads; the 'by' window ends at a clauseBreaks character but reads on across a line break.
negatorWhy: A negated passive denies the act instead of hiding its doer: 'Your data was never sold', 'Passwords have not been compromised', 'No customer data was accessed', 'None of the records were leaked', 'No credit card numbers, bank account details or passwords were stolen'. So a negator anywhere in the clause before the auxiliary leaves the passive unmarked: in the auxiliary chain, as the head word, or before it however long the subject is; and 'never' is no adverb here. 'cannot' is listed because 'can not' and 'can't' already negate. The clause starts after the last headStops character (. ; : ! ? or a line break), or at the start of the text; a comma does not start one, because a long subject is a comma list. Reading the whole clause cannot tell a subject's negator from one in a negated main clause or in an earlier coordinate clause, so it also silences 'There is no evidence that this information has been misused' and 'We do not believe their information has been stolen', which deny the act, and 'No one called, but data were stolen', which does not: under-marking is the safe direction, and measurement/contrast.json records that miss. A negator after the participle ('was shared with no one') is not read.

headWhy.challenge: Nouns that name a challenge someone made: 'concerns were raised' deletes who raised them. Software raises an error and a threat level is raised, so 'raised' after any other noun is not marked.
headWhy.data: Nouns that name someone's data. After them, 'shared', 'sold' and 'disclosed' say the data went to someone else; after any other noun the same verbs are routine ('the slides were shared').
headWhy.dummy: Only the impersonal 'it': 'it was decided' deletes who decided, while 'the date was agreed' or 'the case was decided' names what, in an ordinary passive.
headWhy.error: Nouns that a light verb turns into a deletion: an error ('mistakes were made'), a decision or statement ('remarks were made', 'decisions were taken'), or a step, measure, safeguard, promise or threat an organisation takes or gives ('steps were taken', 'promises were given'). The class is named for its first members; it holds deeds as well as errors.
headWhy.held: Nouns that name something held in trust for someone: the 'data' class's nouns, plus 'account' and 'accounts', so that 'your account was affected' is marked while patients, flights and crops that were affected are not. The account nouns were added for 'affected' and 'impacted' alone (lexicon version 2); the data class was not widened with them, so 'your account was shared' stays unmarked. That is a choice no measurement has tested, in the safe direction.

classes.why: The participle itself names a fault: someone mishandled, misjudged, neglected or tampered.
The participle names a breach of something held in trust, mostly someone's data.

classes.head: held
classes.why: 'Affected' and 'impacted' name a breach only of something held in trust for someone: their data, their account. Patients, flights, earnings, crops and power supplies are affected by causes, not doers, so after any other head noun these words are not marked.
The participle names a concealment or a withdrawal someone decided on.

classes.head: error
classes.why: A light verb says little alone; after an error, decision or statement noun it is the classic deletion ('mistakes were made', 'steps were taken').

classes.head: challenge
classes.why: 'Concerns were raised' deletes the accuser. After any other noun 'raised' is no deletion: software raises an error ('an error was raised'), and a threat level is raised.

classes.head: dummy
classes.why: Only the impersonal 'it was decided' deletes who decided.

classes.head: data
classes.why: After a data noun, these verbs say the data went to someone else: the act the taxonomy's lesson 'your data was shared' names.

excluded.why: Present, modal and progressive passives ('is executed', 'can be frozen', 'were being withheld') describe procedure or ongoing state far more often than a deleted doer; every held-out false positive of the earlier detector was present or modal.
A get-passive is also an idiom ('got fired up', 'got lost'); the words alone cannot tell them apart.
Harm and news verbs: 'Lives were lost in the earthquake', 'Your account was closed at your request'. The words alone cannot say a doer exists, so the rule marks nothing.

Routine data handling: methods sections, retention notices and transfer logs use them as procedure ('Data were collected from 200 participants.', 'Records were retained for seven years.', 'Data were transferred to a secure server.'). The words alone say no harm, fault or concealment.
